title: Olives
question: How do you pick olives?
decision: Olives cured in brine, which ferments them slowly.
why: Fresh olives are bitter, and curing removes it. Brine curing ferments the fruit slowly, with water and salt.
short_answer: Olives off the tree are very bitter, so they are cured before eating. Brine-cured olives ferment slowly in water and salt. Lye-cured olives are a milder style. Opened olives keep about 2 weeks.
detail: Olives picked off the tree hold a very bitter compound called oleuropein. Curing leaches it out. The common cures are water, brine, lye and dry salt, and each gives a different texture and flavor. Water-cured olives stay slightly bitter, because water removes less oleuropein. Brine curing is a fermentation that turns the fruit’s sugars into lactic and acetic acids. It uses only water and salt, but takes a long time. Lye curing works quickly, and rinsing leaves a neutral olive that takes on flavors from vinegar and herbs. Salt gives olives their flavor and serves as a preservative. Salt curing has roots in ancient antiquity. Commercial table olives follow three main methods: Greek, Spanish and Californian. Greek-style olives are picked near full ripeness, at the purple stage, and cured in brine. Spanish-style green olives are treated with lye, rinsed, then fermented. California-style black ripe olives are lye-cured and darkened with air, then colored black with an iron salt. One review’s table puts debittering at 6–12 months for Greek, 1–7 months for Spanish and 1 week for California. The California method gives the mildest flavor and the least bitterness. USDA grade standards cover canned ripe olives (U.S. Grade A, B and C). USDA defines green olives as “completely fermented and cured” fruit of the olive tree.
kristy_take: Cured the slow way, in brine, olives keep a salty, acidic, fermented flavor. Salt curing has roots in antiquity.
buying_tips: Read the jar for the cure: brine, lye or dry salt.
Greek-style olives are near-ripe purple fruit cured in brine.
Spanish-style green olives are treated with lye, rinsed, then fermented.
California-style black ripe olives are the mildest and least bitter: a style, not a flaw.
Finish an opened jar within about 2 weeks.
watch_out: Some Greek-style olives were briefly exposed to air to darken the fruit, with the color set by ferrous gluconate.

labels_decoded.meaning: Sodium hydroxide, used to cure olives quickly; rinsing removes it.
The chemical name for lye on an olive label.
An iron salt that sets the dark color of the fruit.
Canned olives oxidized in processing to a dark brown to black color.
A USDA quality grade for canned ripe olives; Grades B and C also exist.

tier_note: An opened jar keeps about 2 weeks; brine curing is a craft choice.
_do_line: Check the jar date, and finish an opened jar within 2 weeks.
